Kṛtyakalpataru
(‘wish-yielding tree of rituals’)
------------------------------------------
Rituals and sacraments of modern Hindu society depend to a great extent on the पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस् including the निबन्धस् or digests. The Kṛtyakalpataru—more popularly known as Kalpataru—of लक्ष्मीधर (12th century A. D.) is one such nibandha which is both voluminous and also considered as an authority especially in मिथिला, Bengal, Northern and Western India.
Lakṣmīdhara was the son of भट्ट Hṛdayadhara and was the minister for peace and war (called ‘sandhivigrahika’) of the king Govindacandra of Kanauj who ruled from A.

.
The work comprises fourteen kāṇḍas dealing with a variety of subjects as follows:
Kāṇḍa Name Contents
1. Brahmacārikāṇḍa Duties of a brahma-cārin or a Vedic student.
2. Gṛhasthakāṇḍa Duties of a गृहस्थ or a householder.
3. Āhnikakāṇḍa Daily duties like सन्ध्या and pañca-महायज्ञस्.
4. Śrāddhakāṇḍa Obsequial rites.
5. Dānakāṇḍa Giving of gifts.
6. Vratakāṇḍa Vratas or religious rites based mostly on the पुराणस्.
7. Pūjākāṇḍa Worship, consecra-tion of temples and images.
8. Tīrthavivecana- kāṇḍa Pilgrimage to holy places like काशी, प्रयाग, गया and so on.
9. Prāyaścittakāṇḍa Expiatory rites.
10. Śuddhikāṇḍa Aśauca (ceremonial impurity) and ways of remedying it.
11. Rājadharmakāṇḍa Coronation of the king,, on ministers,, forts and palaces,, administration of the State and so on.
12. Vyavahārakāṇḍa Law and administra-tion of justice.
13. Śāntikakāṇḍa Śāntis or propitiatory rites for averting a deity’s wrath or evil effects of a planet.
14. Mokṣakāṇḍa Liberation as per Advaita Vedānta.

Lakṣmīdhara might have composed his work during the period A.

Kṛtayuga
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस्, while describing च्रेअतिओन् and allied topics, give us some idea of the concept of time in the ancient days. ‘Yuga’ is one such concept.
The युगस् are four in number. They are: कृतयुग, त्रेतायुग, द्वापरयुग and कलियुग.
The Kṛtayuga—also called ‘Satya-yuga’—is spread over 4800 years of the gods or 17,28,000 human years.
It is supposed to begin on that day when Ravi (the sun), चन्द्र (the मोओन्) and बृहस्पति or गुरु (the जुपितेर्) meet in the नक्षत्र or asterism of पुष्य (gamma, delta, theta cancri).
In this yuga, धर्म (conceived of as a bull) is firmly established on all the four feet. People are well-fed, well-clothed, ever satisfied and happy. They are always rooted in धर्म and never swerve from it. Members of the four varṇas are ever devoted to their vocations. There is perfect harmony in the society.
See also DVĀPARAYUGA, KALIYUGA, TRETĀYUGA and YUGAS.

Kṛtyaratnākara
(‘ocean of religious observances’)
------------------------------------------
The Kṛtyaratnākara is one of the seven sections of the voluminous nibandha or digest, the Smṛtiratnākara or simply, the Ratnākara by चण्डेश्वर. (See CAṆḌEŚVARA.)
It has 22 taraṅgas (sub-sections) dealing with the nature of धर्म, various vratas and other religious observances including rites to be performed on एच्लिप्से days.
The Ratnākara has influenced greatly, the writers of धर्मशास्त्रस् and निबन्धस् from मिथिला (North Bihar) and Bengal.

Kṛttikā
------------------------------------------
It is a नक्षत्र or asterism, third in the series of 27 nakṣatras. It is actually a group of six स्तर्स् known as the pleiades. Persons born under this नक्षत्र are considered as demoniacal in nature.
These six स्तर्स् are described in the पुराणस् as six goddesses who simultaneously suckled the baby सुब्रह्मण्य who assumed six heads and hence came to be known as षण्मुख or the Six faced one.
As per the Taittirīya Saṁhitā and the Atharvaveda, this नक्षत्र was the first in the series. Some scholars have therefore attempted to fix the date of the Vedic Saṁhitās on the assumption that the vernal equinox occurred at that time when the sun was in कृत्तिका.
See also NAKṢATRAS.
